facts.text: Blood Freak's budget was reportedly just $25,000, and it still managed a turkey-headed drug-fiend monster, a table-saw amputation and a sermon or two.
Star Steve Hawkes took this job to pay skin-graft bills after being badly burned on the set of a Tarzan movie in Florida. His scarred arms reportedly show up in some Blood Freak scenes.
Classic-Horror.com's Nate Yapp says the gore here is cherry Kool-Aid, and the severed limb is plastic. Not exactly corn-syrup-and-latex Hollywood craftsmanship.
Steve Hawkes was born Stjepan Šipek in Croatia. He came to America to make Spanish-language Tarzan movies for the South American market before ending up as a turkey-headed junkie.
The lead character's name, Herschell, is a tribute to gore-film pioneer Herschell Gordon Lewis, the 'Godfather of Gore' behind Blood Feast.
Most of the cast were acting students from co-director Brad F. Grinter's class. Grinter reportedly used some of his students' tuition money to fund his own film projects.
The original financier reportedly backed out partway through shooting. Co-directors Brad F. Grinter and Steve Hawkes finished the film with their own money.
Co-director Brad F. Grinter also made Flesh Feast (1970), the final film appearance of Hollywood star Veronica Lake. She died in 1973.
Before Blood Freak, director Brad F. Grinter made several 'nudie-cuties' shot at Florida nudist camps. He was himself a nudist, according to TCM.
The video box billed it as 'the world's first turkey-monster-pro-jesus-anti-drug-gore-film,' according to Classic-Horror.com's review. Every word of that is accurate.
Years later, star Steve Hawkes called Blood Freak 'a sad chapter in my life.'
The film was originally rated X for its violence. It was re-edited in 1975 to earn an R rating from the MPAA.
The man who loses a leg to a table saw was reportedly played by a real amputee, one of Brad F. Grinter's acting students.
The turkey head worn by star Steve Hawkes was made of papier-mâché.
PopMatters writer Bill Gibron called Blood Freak the only exploitation film endorsed by the Southern Baptist Convention, the Betty Ford Clinic and the Butterball Thanksgiving Hotline.
The film's tagline billed it as 'A Dracula On Drugs!'
PopMatters writer Bill Gibron listed Blood Freak as a guilty pleasure. He praised its 'endless shots of Grinter babbling like an improvising, smut peddling Criswell.'
Dennis Schwartz of Ozus' World Movie Reviews gave it a C+ and called everything about it 'Ed Wood bad.' He said it demands to be seen by weird film addicts.
Casey Scott of DVD Drive-In described Blood Freak as a mix of a Ron Ormond Christian message film, an H.G. Lewis gorefest and an anti-pot PSA.
Bleeding Skull's Joseph A. Ziemba called it 'a trash film revelation. Peerless, disturbed, and completely stupid.'
The sound is non-synchronized, with clucking noises, a recurring shriek and one heavily reused musical sting, according to a Gizmodo write-up of the film.
Gizmodo noted that director Brad F. Grinter, who plays the film's narrator, smokes on camera and seems to read his lines from a table.
Blood Freak has been name-checked in later films, including Blood Sucking Freaks (1976), Nail Gun Massacre (2009) and Happy Thanksgiving (2023).
In 2004, star Steve Hawkes's pet tiger Bobo escaped his Florida animal compound and was shot dead the next day, making national news. Hawkes believes it was needless.
Gizmodo's Cheryl Eddy called Blood Freak a 'craptacular masterpiece' and argued it 'is what Thanksgiving traditions should be built upon.'
Steve Hawkes and his animal sanctuary were featured on The Daily Show in 1999.
Years after Blood Freak, star Steve Hawkes returned to horror with the zombie films 2056 Escape from Zombie Island (2012) and 2057: Return to Zombie Island (2013).
Grinter's cast included his own family. His son Randy Grinter, a cameraman, appears in the film. His daughter Heather Grinter is credited too, as Angel.
Director Brad F. Grinter later retired to a Christian life in Florida and died in 1993.
The film's Hollywood-ish blend of Christian message, gore and anti-drug sermon has made it a cult Thanksgiving favorite among horror fans.
Reviewer Nate Yapp wrote that Ed Wood 'would have been mighty proud' of Blood Freak, though he still found Plan 9 from Outer Space the better-constructed film.
